walkthroughs.body_html:
Plant Biology — a core area of Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Plant Biology brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Plant Biology.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Munch's pressure flow hypothesis for phloem transport dates from:

options: Cytokinin
Auxin (IAA)
Ethylene
Abscisic acid

mcqs.q: What makes the antigen-binding site of an antibody specific to one antigen?
options: All antibodies have the same binding site; specificity comes from where they go in the body.
The left ventricle is thicker because it is on the same side as the brain.
The variable region — its amino acid sequence (and thus shape) differs between antibodies, complementing a specific antigen.
Antibodies bind to any antigen they meet first.

mcqs.q: What is produced in anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells?
options: Anaerobic respiration produces oxygen as a waste product.
Antibodies bind to any antigen they meet first.
Anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and CO2 in humans.
Lactic acid (lactate) and a small amount of ATP — no CO2 or water in this pathway.

mcqs.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker muscular wall than the right?
options: Anaerobic respiration produces oxygen as a waste product.
It must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body; the right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs.
The left ventricle is thicker because it handles oxygenated blood, which is harder to pump.
The left ventricle is thicker because it is on the same side as the brain.
